Discovery merger -- agreeing to a five-year court-enforceable package of at least $1.5bn of extra domestic film spend, 30 then 32 theatrical releases a year with a $30m payment per film missed, a $47.5m worker fund, a five-year ban on selling or closing the Los Angeles studio lots, separate cable-carriage negotiations and an independent board over CBS News and CNN; no divestitures, and closing is now guided to early October (approved → approved) (psky-wbd-acquisition)

NEW: Artemis Gold is issuing 0.0966 of its own shares per Vista Gold share -- US$2.83 a share, US$427m, a 29% premium -- to buy the permitted but unbuilt 10.5m-ounce Mt Todd project in Australia's Northern Territory and a stated path past a million ounces a year, paying in paper today for ounces that still need a large capex decision (artg-vista-gold-acquisition)

NEW: Generac has signed a long-term backup-power agreement with Amazon worth $2.4bn of committed deliveries in 2027-28 and up to $8bn over its life, against roughly $4bn of annual group revenue, granting Amazon warrants over up to 1,693,745 shares at $200.93 that vest as it pays for generators -- the stock re-rated more than 40% and hyperscaler capex replaced the housing cycle as the swing factor in earnings (gnrc-amazon-generator-supply)

themes.label: Public-to-private buyout offers on listed companies
themes.note: Sponsors, strategics and cooperatives keep taking listed businesses off public markets, and London remains the densest hunting ground: Veritas Capital's 940p a share for Bodycote after outbidding CVC in an auction that also drew Apollo (boy-veritas-take-private) and Epiris's 1,120p for Gamma Communications at a 53% premium, structured as a court-sanctioned scheme completing in H1 2027 (gama-epiris-take-private) -- both profitable mid-caps the public market rated a third or more below what private capital would pay. The contested approaches are still open rather than resolved: Uber's EUR41.50-a-share, ~EUR13bn tender for Delivery Hero carries a formal board recommendation and runs to 5 November on a minimum of only 50% plus one share, with Prosus's ~17% irrevocably committed (dher-uber-takeover-offer); Curaleaf's hostile tender for Aurora Cannabis runs to 1 December against a board circular telling holders to reject, and both sides have now filed complaints with the Alberta Securities Commission (acb-curaleaf-takeover-bid); and Deoleo's board has handed Coricelli exclusivity at EUR500m while the Spanish bidders refuse to concede (ole-coricelli-takeover-bid). Where two bidders show up, the auction rather than the opening offer sets the exit -- DNO's $5.214 a share for Capricorn Energy topped Genel's recommended bid by about 10% and flipped the board (cne-dno-acquisition). The smallest approach is the most conflicted: Advent International, already Definitive Healthcare's controlling owner, has put a non-binding $1.02-a-share all-cash proposal to a special committee of independent directors for the stock it and founder Jason Krantz do not hold, which makes the committee, not the premium, the only thing standing between minority holders and a take-under (dh-advent-take-private). The two most recent US cases show the whole spread in one week: Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell's DFO Management are paying $32.50 a share for Baldwin, an 88% premium to its unaffected June price and a $7.7bn enterprise value, while H.I.G. is taking MISTRAS at $20.35, an $866m enterprise value carrying a premium of just 8% to the 30-day VWAP (bwin-sequence-dfo-take-private, mg-hig-take-private). Both targets had already re-rated hard -- Baldwin up 58% in three months, MISTRAS up 61% since the end of 2025 -- so in one case the sponsor paid for the rest of the runway and in the other the stock's own rally supplied almost all of the exit price, with 31% of the MISTRAS register locked into support agreements and a go-shop to 27 October as the only route to more. Two deals are now effectively done: Abu Dhabi's L'imad has met every condition of its AED6.25-a-share offer for AD Ports and, with acceptances for another 23.08%, will own more than 98.5% and delist the port operator once settlement completes by 9 October (adports-limad-takeover-bid), while Copart is tendering $10.50 a share in cash for ACV Auctions, a 45% premium that takes a listed digital-auction rival off the market (cprt-acv-acquisition).

themes.label: AI data-center capacity and power build-out
themes.note: Capital keeps flowing to the physical layer of AI compute, and the bottleneck keeps moving down the stack to power, cooling and silicon supply. Getting power onto a site is the scarcest input, and Vertiv paid for it directly: $1.45bn cash plus up to $1.15bn of earnout for UtilityInnovation Group's microgrid controls, on-site generation orchestration and behind-the-meter architecture, explicitly framed as shortening time-to-power for customers who can build a data center faster than a utility can energise it (vrt-utilityinnovation-acquisition). Amazon has gone one step further and contracted the generators themselves, committing $2.4bn across 2027-28 and up to $8bn over the life of a backup-power agreement with Generac -- a company whose franchise was suburban home standby until this deal made hyperscaler capex its swing factor (gnrc-amazon-generator-supply). The pull now reaches the regulated utilities themselves, and with them the politics: NextEra's $67bn all-stock purchase of Dominion, the largest regulated utility deal ever announced, is being fought in Virginia over exactly who pays for data-center load growth, and the September concession package funds four years of residential bill credits by redirecting credits that would otherwise have gone to data centers (nee-dominion-acquisition). Upstream in gas supply, SOCAR is paying Comstock $1.65bn for working interests in the Haynesville, the basin feeding Gulf Coast LNG and the power demand behind it (crk-socar-haynesville-partnership). At the silicon layer the buildout has produced its first credible second source for inference: AWS may take up to $60bn of Qualcomm custom inference chips and 1.6Tbps optical interconnect over ten years (qcom-aws-ai-chip-deal).

themes.label: Signed M&A deals hitting regulatory or legal roadblocks
themes.note: Deals investors thought were settled keep being resolved by regulators, politicians and shareholder ballots rather than by the parties -- and the largest of them has just shown what that costs. Paramount's $111bn purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery had cleared 68 jurisdictions and still could not close until the 12-state antitrust suit was settled; on 21 September it was, but the price was a five-year court-enforceable behavioural package -- $1.5bn of extra domestic film spend, a 30-then-32 annual release floor with a $30m payment for each film missed, a $47.5m worker fund, a five-year ban on selling the Los Angeles lots, separate cable-carriage negotiations and an independent board over CBS News and CNN, policed by a five-state committee. No divestitures, so the asset base arrives intact, but the commitments are now fixed charges on the synergy case (psky-wbd-acquisition). NextEra-Dominion is the unresolved version: every economic term is agreed, yet the deal turns on Virginia's State Corporation Commission, and the companies have already doubled residential bill relief to four years, lifted the credit pool from $1.78bn to $1.87bn and added $100m to Dominion's hardship programme to buy approval -- margin given away before closing, with no guarantee it is the last concession (nee-dominion-acquisition). Uber's agreed, board-recommended tender for Delivery Hero shows how long the tail runs even when nobody is fighting: merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances across a 99-country footprint push guided settlement into the second half of 2027 (dher-uber-takeover-offer). Nvidia's signed $12.93bn purchase of Hugging Face faces full merger review in the US, EU and likely the UK on whether it would tilt a neutral model hub toward its own silicon, which is why the open-platform commitment was made on day one (nvda-huggingface-acquisition). In Canada the regulator has been drafted into the fight itself, with Curaleaf asking the Alberta Securities Commission to halt Aurora's at-the-market issuance during the offer while Aurora files its own complaint about the bid's deficiencies (acb-curaleaf-takeover-bid), and in Spain the agriculture ministry keeps arguing publicly that the world's largest olive-oil bottler should end up with a domestic buyer even as the board grants an Italian one exclusivity (ole-coricelli-takeover-bid).

themes.label: Financial firms buying platforms and product lines rather than building them
themes.note: Companies keep concluding that the capabilities the market now pays for are quicker to buy than to build, and that what they are buying is a distribution platform or a fee stream rather than assets. The pattern is now mostly cross-border: Samsung Life is negotiating a ~15% stake in Principal Financial Group for $3.6-4.4bn, enough to displace Vanguard as the largest holder of a manager running $808bn and administering 401(k) plans for ~11.3m participants (samsung-life-principal-financial-stake), while Samsung Fire & Marine negotiates the ~60% of Lloyd's specialty insurer Canopius it does not already own (samsung-fire-canopius-buyout) -- a US retirement distribution platform and a Lloyd's underwriting licence bought rather than built at home, in what would together be the largest cross-border acquisition a Korean financial group has done. Grab has done the same thing one layer down the stack, paying $1.49bn for 60% of Atome Financial to buy a working BNPL, cards and digital-lending platform across five Southeast Asian markets rather than originating its own book from scratch (grab-atome-acquisition). In each case the buyer is acquiring reach and licences it could not assemble organically, and taking on the underwriting or credit risk that comes attached. The domestic version is Aon's $17bn all-cash purchase of USI's middle-market brokerage platform from KKR, now funded with a $13.5bn seven-part bond sale that drew about $65bn of orders -- which puts the price of buying rather than building on Aon's own balance sheet (aon-usi-acquisition).

themes.label: Hyperscalers taking warrants in the suppliers they commit to
themes.note: Amazon has now twice paid for scarce AI-infrastructure supply partly in the supplier's own equity, and in both cases the warrants vest against purchases rather than at signing, so the customer is compensated for the volume it actually delivers. Qualcomm granted Amazon warrants worth about $4bn, struck at $161.26, alongside an agreement under which AWS may buy up to $60bn of custom inference silicon and 1.6Tbps optical interconnect over ten years (qcom-aws-ai-chip-deal); Generac granted warrants over up to 1,693,745 shares at $200.93, roughly 308,000 exercisable immediately and the rest unlocking as Amazon pays for generators under a $2.4bn-committed, up-to-$8bn backup-power pact (gnrc-amazon-generator-supply). For the supplier the contract is transformative revenue bought with dilution that only bites if the volume arrives; for holders it caps the upside from the very re-rating the announcement triggers -- Generac's stock moved more than 40% on the news, most of which now accrues in part to the counterparty. The template is spreading beyond Amazon, Oracle having taken the same structure in Bloom Energy in April.
